solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.body: Every resident of $T'$ makes two dishes from $\mathrm{dish}(T)\setminus\{D\}$, so $\mathrm{dish}(T')\subseteq\mathrm{dish}(T)\setminus\{D\}$. Take any two dishes $D_i\ne D_j$ in $\mathrm{dish}(T)\setminus\{D\}$. Since $T$ is full, exactly one resident $r$ of $T$ makes both; $r$'s two dishes are $D_i,D_j$, so $r$ does not make $D$ and $r\in T'$. Hence $\mathrm{dish}(T')=\mathrm{dish}(T)\setminus\{D\}$ (when at least two dishes remain), every pair of these dishes is made by a resident of $T'$, and by exactly one, since $T$ has only one such resident. So $T'$ is full. ∎

A **$D$-chef** is a resident who knows how to make dish $D$, and $\mathrm{chef}_T(D)$ is the set of $D$-chefs in $T$.

Prove that for any town $T$,
$$\sum_{D\in\mathrm{dish}(T)}|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|=2\,\mathrm{pop}(T).$$
answer: Double-count the resident–dish pairs $(r,D)$ with $r$ making $D$.

solutions.title: Double counting
solutions.body: Let $\mathcal S=\{(r,D): r\in T,\ D\in\mathrm{dish}(T),\ r\text{ makes }D\}$. Counting by dishes, each $D$ contributes $|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|$ pairs, so $|\mathcal S|=\sum_D|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|$. Counting by residents, each resident makes exactly two dishes, so $|\mathcal S|=2\,\mathrm{pop}(T)$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Question 2014: Power of Potlucks.)* In each town in ARMLandia, every resident knows how to make **exactly two dishes**, and no two residents of a town know how to make the same pair of dishes. The population $\mathrm{pop}(T)$ of a town $T$ is its number of residents, and $\mathrm{dish}(T)$ is the set of dishes its residents collectively know how to make. A town $T$ is **full** if for every pair of dishes in $\mathrm{dish}(T)$ there is exactly one resident who knows how to make those two dishes; $\mathcal F_d$ denotes a full town with $|\mathrm{dish}(\mathcal F_d)|=d$. A **resident cycle** is a sequence of distinct residents $r_1,\dots,r_n$ such that $r_i$ and $r_{i+1}$ know a common dish for $1\le i\le n-1$, $r_n$ and $r_1$ know a common dish, and no other pair $r_i,r_j$ knows a common dish. Two resident cycles are indistinguishable if they contain the same residents (in any order).

Compute the number of distinguishable resident cycles of length 6 in $\mathcal F_8$.

solutions.title: Cycles of dishes
solutions.body:
Identify each resident with the pair of dishes he or she makes. In a resident cycle of length $6$, consecutive residents share a dish, and the shared dishes must all be different (if $r_{i-1},r_i$ and $r_i,r_{i+1}$ shared the same dish, then $r_{i-1}$ and $r_{i+1}$ would share it too). So the cycle looks like $(d_1d_2),(d_2d_3),\dots,(d_6d_1)$ with $d_1,\dots,d_6$ distinct: a 6-cycle on the dishes.

There are $8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=20160$ ordered choices of $(d_1,\dots,d_6)$; each cycle is counted $6$ times (starting point) $\times2$ (direction). So there are $\frac{20160}{12}=1680$ cycles.

**Answer: 1680**

prompt:

The population $\mathrm{pop}(T)$ of a town $T$ is its number of residents, and $\mathrm{dish}(T)$ is the set of dishes its residents collectively know how to make. A town $T$ is **full** if for every pair of dishes in $\mathrm{dish}(T)$ there is exactly one resident who knows how to make those two dishes; $\mathcal F_d$ denotes a full town with $|\mathrm{dish}(\mathcal F_d)|=d$. A **resident cycle** is a sequence of distinct residents $r_1,\dots,r_n$ such that $r_i$ and $r_{i+1}$ know a common dish for $1\le i\le n-1$, $r_n$ and $r_1$ know a common dish, and no other pair $r_i,r_j$ knows a common dish. Two resident cycles are indistinguishable if they contain the same residents (in any order).

In terms of $k$ and $d$, find the number of distinguishable resident cycles of length $k$ in $\mathcal F_d$.
answer: $\dfrac{d(d-1)\cdots(d-k+1)}{2k}=\dfrac{d!}{2k\,(d-k)!}$ (for $k\ge4$; for $k=3$ this counts the "triangles" $d_1d_2,d_2d_3,d_3d_1$).

solutions.title: Generalise 8a
solutions.body:
As in 8a, for $k\ge4$ a resident cycle of length $k$ is $(d_1d_2),(d_2d_3),\dots,(d_kd_1)$ with distinct dishes $d_1,\dots,d_k$: if $r_{i-1}$ and $r_{i+1}$ shared the dish common to $r_i$, they'd be a forbidden non-consecutive pair. There are $d(d-1)\cdots(d-k+1)$ ordered choices, and each cycle arises from $k$ starting points and $2$ directions, giving
$$\frac{d(d-1)\cdots(d-k+1)}{2k}=\frac{d!}{2k\,(d-k)!}.$$

*Remark on $k=3$:* here every pair of residents is consecutive, so besides the $\frac{d(d-1)(d-2)}{6}$ triangles $(d_1d_2),(d_2d_3),(d_3d_1)$, three residents who all make one common dish, such as $(d_1d_2),(d_1d_3),(d_1d_4)$, also satisfy the definition literally; there are $d\binom{d-1}{3}$ of these. The official answer is the formula above.

reviewNote: Official answer d!/(2k(d-k)!) is right for k >= 4; for k = 3 the literal definition also admits "stars" (three residents sharing one dish), which the official count omits. Solution mentions this.

A **resident cycle** is a sequence of distinct residents $r_1,\dots,r_n$ such that $r_i$ and $r_{i+1}$ know a common dish for $1\le i\le n-1$, $r_n$ and $r_1$ know a common dish, and no other pair $r_i,r_j$ knows a common dish. Two resident cycles are indistinguishable if they contain the same residents (in any order).

Let $T$ be a town with at least two residents that has a single resident cycle that contains every resident. Prove that $T$ is homogeneous if and only if $\mathrm{pop}(T)$ is even.
answer: With the cycle $r_1,\dots,r_n$, each dish has at most 2 chefs; alternate groups 1, 2 work iff $n$ is even, and an odd cycle can't be 2-coloured. (Exception: three residents sharing one common dish.)

solutions.title: Two-colour the cycle
solutions.body:
Let the cycle be $r_1,\dots,r_n$ ($n=\mathrm{pop}(T)$), so the only pairs sharing a dish are $r_ir_{i+1}$ and $r_nr_1$.

**Each dish has at most two chefs** (when $n\ne3$, or $n=3$ with no dish common to all three): if three residents made the same dish, every two of them would share it, but for $n\ge4$ among any three residents of the cycle some two are non-consecutive. (For $n=2$, the two residents make different pairs of dishes, so they share exactly one dish.) Also some dish has exactly $2$ chefs, namely a dish shared by $r_1$ and $r_2$. Hence $\max_D|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|=2$, and $T$ is homogeneous iff $\mathrm{gr}(T)=2$.

**$n$ even:** put $r_i$ in group 1 for odd $i$ and group 2 for even $i$. Every conflicting pair $r_ir_{i+1}$ or $r_nr_1$ ($n$ even, $1$ odd) gets different groups. So $\mathrm{gr}(T)\le2$, hence $=2$: homogeneous.

**$n$ odd:** with only two groups, consecutive residents alternate groups, so $r_i$ is in the group of $r_1$ exactly for odd $i$; then $r_n$ ($n$ odd) is in $r_1$'s group although they share a dish. Contradiction, so $\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge3>2$: heterogeneous. ∎

Then $|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|=3=\mathrm{gr}(T)$ and the town is homogeneous although $\mathrm{pop}(T)=3$ is odd; the statement (and the official solution) implicitly exclude this case.

Two resident cycles are indistinguishable if they contain the same residents (in any order).

Let $T$ be a town such that, for each $D\in\mathrm{dish}(T)$, $|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|=2$. Prove that there are finitely many resident cycles $C_1,C_2,\dots,C_j$ in $T$ so that each resident belongs to exactly one of the $C_i$.
answer: Follow dishes: from a resident, go to the other chef of one of his dishes, and continue; the walk must close up into a cycle; remove it and induct.

solutions.title: Every dish has degree 2
solutions.body:
Build a graph $G$ whose vertices are the dishes and whose edges are the residents: resident $r$ is the edge joining his two dishes. No two residents make the same pair, so $G$ has no repeated edges, and two residents share a dish iff their edges share an endpoint. Every dish has exactly two chefs, so every vertex of $G$ has degree exactly $2$.

**Each connected component of $G$ is a cycle.** In a component, take a longest path $v_0v_1\cdots v_t$ (with distinct vertices). $v_0$ has a second neighbour besides $v_1$; it lies on the path (otherwise the path could be extended), and it can't be $v_j$ with $1<j<t$ ($v_j$ already has the two neighbours $v_{j-1},v_{j+1}$). So it is $v_t$, and $t\ge2$ (no repeated edges). Now every $v_j$ has its two edges inside the closed cycle $v_0v_1\cdots v_tv_0$, so no other edge touches these vertices and the component is exactly this cycle.

**Each cycle of $G$ is a resident cycle.** If the cycle has dishes $v_0,\dots,v_t$, its edges are the residents $s_1=v_0v_1,\ s_2=v_1v_2,\dots,s_{t+1}=v_tv_0$. Consecutive residents share a dish; non-consecutive ones share no endpoint (for $t+1\ge4$; for $t+1=3$ all pairs are consecutive); and no other resident shares a dish with them, since each $v_j$ has degree $2$.

The components are finite in number and disjoint, so the residents split into finitely many resident cycles $C_1,\dots,C_j$, each resident in exactly one. ∎

Let $T$ be a town such that, for each $D\in\mathrm{dish}(T)$, $|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|=2$. answer: Some cycle in the decomposition has odd length, and an odd cycle can't be split into two groups; so $\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge3>2$.

solutions.title: An odd cycle
solutions.body:
All dishes have exactly $2$ chefs, so $T$ is homogeneous iff $\mathrm{gr}(T)=2$, and heterogeneous iff $\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge3$.

Split $T$ into resident cycles. Their lengths add up to the odd number $\mathrm{pop}(T)$, so some cycle $r_1,\dots,r_{2k+1}$ has odd length ($k\ge1$). Suppose $f:T\to\{1,2\}$ were a group assignment. Consecutive residents of the cycle share a dish, so $f(r_{i+1})\ne f(r_i)$, i.e. $f$ alternates: $f(r_i)=f(r_1)$ for all odd $i$. In particular $f(r_{2k+1})=f(r_1)$, but $r_{2k+1}$ and $r_1$ share a dish. Contradiction. Hence $\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge3>2=|\mathrm{chef}_T(D)|$ for all $D$, and $T$ is heterogeneous. ∎

solutions.title: Colour the cycle in two colours, everyone else in a third
solutions.body:
$\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge3$ by problem 6. Let the cycle be $C=r_1,\dots,r_n$.

**Degenerate case $n=3$ with a common dish.** If $r_1,r_2,r_3$ all make one dish $D$, say $(D,a),(D,b),(D,c)$, then $\mathrm{dish}(T)=\{D,a,b,c\}$ (every dish has a chef in $C$). Each of $a,b,c$ needs two more chefs, who make only dishes among $a,b,c$; the only such residents are $(a,b),(a,c),(b,c)$, each at most once, and they supply exactly the $6$ needed chef slots. So $T=\mathcal F_4$, and $\mathrm{gr}(T)=3$ by problem 3a.

**Otherwise** each dish made by a resident of $C$ is made by exactly two residents of $C$, and they are consecutive: for $n\ge4$, the dishes $r_i$ shares with $r_{i-1}$ and with $r_{i+1}$ must differ (else $r_{i-1},r_{i+1}$ would share), so both of $r_i$'s dishes are shared with neighbours; a third chef in $C$ would create a non-consecutive pair. (For $n=3$ without a common dish the same holds.) Counting chef slots in $C$: $2n=2|\mathrm{dish}(T)|$, so $n=|\mathrm{dish}(T)|$, which is even (problem 11a), and $n\ge4$.

Define $f(r)=1$ for $r\notin C$, $f(r_i)=2$ for even $i$, $f(r_i)=3$ for odd $i$. Take any dish $D$: its $3$ chefs are two consecutive residents of $C$ (consecutive in the cyclic order; $r_n,r_1$ are also fine since $n$ is even) and one resident outside $C$. These get three different groups. So no two residents sharing a dish share a group, $f$ is a group assignment, and $\mathrm{gr}(T)=3$. ∎

solutions.title: Pairing the dishes
solutions.body: Suppose a group $R$ contains a $D$-chef for every dish $D$. Members of a group share no dishes, so each dish is made by exactly one member of $R$. Each member makes exactly two dishes, so the dishes are partitioned into the pairs $\{$the two dishes of $r\}$, $r\in R$. Then $|\mathrm{dish}(T)|=2|R|$ is even, a contradiction. ∎

solutions.title: One group plus k more
solutions.body: Let $f$ be a group assignment and $R=f^{-1}(1)$. Some dish $D$ has no chef in $R$. The $k$ chefs of $D$ pairwise share $D$, so they lie in $k$ distinct groups, none of which is group $1$. So $f$ uses at least $k+1$ groups, and $\mathrm{gr}(T)\ge k+1>k$. ∎

(Earlier results: if every dish of a town $T$ has exactly $k$ chefs and $|\mathrm{dish}(T)|$ is odd, then $\mathrm{gr}(T)>k$.) For each odd positive integer $d\ge3$, prove that $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)=d$.
answer: Each dish has $d-1$ chefs, so $\mathrm{gr}>d-1$; the assignment $f(r_{ij})\equiv i+j\pmod d$ uses $d$ groups.

solutions.title: Lower bound and the i+j colouring
solutions.body:
Label the dishes $D_1,\dots,D_d$ and let $r_{ij}$ ($i<j$) be the resident who makes $D_i$ and $D_j$.

**Lower bound.** Each dish $D_i$ is made by the $d-1$ residents $r_{ij}$, $j\ne i$. So every dish has $k=d-1$ chefs and $|\mathrm{dish}|=d$ is odd; by the earlier result $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)>d-1$.

**Upper bound.** Let $f(r_{ij})=(i+j)\bmod d\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$. If two different residents share a dish, say $r_{ij}$ and $r_{i\ell}$ with $j\ne\ell$ (indices written in any order), then $f$ values are $i+j$ and $i+\ell$, which differ mod $d$ because $1\le j,\ell\le d$ and $j\ne\ell$. So $f$ is a group assignment with $d$ groups.

Hence $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)=d$. ∎

A **group assignment** on $T$ is a function $f:T\to\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ such that if $f(r_i)=f(r_j)$ for $i\ne j$, then $r_i$ and $r_j$ do not know any of the same dishes. The **group number** $\mathrm{gr}(T)$ is the least positive integer $k$ for which a group assignment on $T$ exists.

(Earlier results: $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_2)\le\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_3)\le\cdots$, and $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)=d$ for odd $d\ge3$.) For each even positive integer $d$, prove that $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)=d-1$.
answer: $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)\ge\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_{d-1})=d-1$; the "round-robin" assignment $f(r_{ij})=i+j$, $f(r_{id})=2i \pmod{d-1}$ uses $d-1$ groups.

solutions.title: Monotonicity and a round-robin schedule
solutions.body:
Label the dishes $D_1,\dots,D_d$ and let $r_{ij}$ ($i<j$) be the resident who makes $D_i$ and $D_j$.

For $d=2$, $\mathcal F_2$ has one resident and $\mathrm{gr}=1=d-1$. Let $d\ge4$.

**Lower bound.** By monotonicity and the odd case, $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)\ge\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_{d-1})=d-1$. (Alternatively, $D_1$ has $d-1$ chefs.)

**Upper bound.** Let $m=d-1$ (odd) and work mod $m$. Define
$$f(r_{ij})\equiv i+j\ \ (1\le i<j\le m),\qquad f(r_{id})\equiv 2i\ \ (1\le i\le m).$$
Check the residents making a fixed dish:
- $D_i$ with $i\le m$: its chefs are $r_{ij}$ ($j\le m$, $j\ne i$) with values $i+j$, and $r_{id}$ with value $2i=i+i$. As $j$ runs over all residues mod $m$ (including $j=i$ via $r_{id}$), the values $i+j$ are all distinct.
- $D_d$: its chefs $r_{id}$ have values $2i$, $i=1,\dots,m$, which are distinct mod $m$ because $m$ is odd ($2$ is invertible).

So any two residents sharing a dish get different values, and $f$ is a group assignment with $m=d-1$ groups. Hence $\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal F_d)=d-1$. ∎

(The official solution instead extends a $(d-1)$-group assignment of $\mathcal F_{d-1}$ by giving $r_{id}$ the unique group missing a $D_i$-chef, and shows by counting that these missing groups are distinct.)
